text.p: A group of top rappers held an impromptu "summit meeting" Wednesday on Howard Stern's radio show to debate whether an east-west rap rivalry is killing famous rappers.
"Is anybody here afraid that they'll be next?" Stern asked the rappers about charges that the rivalry led to the deaths of Tupac Shakur and the Notorious B.I.G, who was also known as Biggie Smalls.
"Negative," said Chubb Rock, who claimed that the rivalry was a media invention.

"The practitioners of this genre right here I think are led into this fictional story of who killed who," he said. "Tupac got into an altercation with people who are not rappers. There have not been any rap suspects in any of these killings."
Stern asked the group, which included Luther Campbell, Boo-Ya Tribe, Grandmaster Mele-Mel, Grandmaster Kay and Daz from Dogg Pound, if rap fans were doing the killings.
"If that were the case," said Chubb Rock, "there should have been a million killings after John Lennon died."
But West Coast rapper Daz, who joined the conference via telephone, wasn't so sure.

"Am I avoiding New York?" he responded to Stern's question. "A lot of people thought when Tupac got shot, that Biggie and his manager had something to do with it. From my standpoint, why would you go to somebody's house after something like that happened? You gotta' let that die out."
Mele-Mel, one of the godfathers of rap who contributed to the earliest rap hit "The Message" 15 years ago, said that the gangsta' rap image is perpetuated by the record industry.

"There are harsh realities but that's not all that's out there," he said. "You go to record companies, if you're not making gangster rap records you're notting getting signed because that's what's hot. So now you have a whole generation of people making gangster records."
Mele-Mel offered a Swiftian solution in keeping with the theme of the Stern program:

"If a guy wants to be a gangster rapper, let him say his rhyme. As soon as he talks about shooting someone, shoot him. If he screams or clutches his wounds, that means he ain't worthy to be a hard core rapper. Some guys try to play extra tough. Nobody's that tough."
In general, however, the tone sounded was a definite note of peace. Cubb Rock talked about a record he released on the subject of the alleged feud, "East-West."
"I just tried to get the message out there that this is total nonsense," he said. "While we're here debating all these crazy issues, we should be on tour doing what we do."
